en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the venerable teacher Prabhākara.
The ninth chapter, adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes on difficult passages.
Word attains the status of a valid means of knowledge when its relationship [to its object] is non-human (apauruṣeya);
and since that [non-human status] would be established only upon the proof of its eternity, that [eternity] is now demonstrated. // 1 //
If a word were to perish immediately upon being uttered, then its innate capacity to denote its own meaning could not be ascertained through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
For it is only by observing repeated usage that one’s ability to denote its specific meaning is determined, having extracted it by excluding various non-relevant meanings.
Furthermore, the observation of repeated application of a word—which ceases as soon as it is uttered—would not be possible [if it were a mere momentary entity].
Moreover, if its capacity to denote its own meaning is not determined, then like a word heard for the first time, it would not be able to cause the understanding of the object.
And since it is improper for that which does not cause the understanding of an object to possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*), [the word must be eternal].
For one who desires the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*), it is proper to establish the eternity of the denotation; thus, this [treatise] serves a purpose.

Now, even if phonemes (*varṇa*) are momentary, the determination of the relationship [between word and meaning] based on the linguistic usage of elders regarding objects such as "g-ness" (*gatva*) is indeed possible; so what is the use of the effort to establish their eternity?

It is said: it is not possible to postulate a universal such as "ga-ness" (*gatva*) with respect to distinct phonemes at every utterance, because even when their difference is not perceived, the conceit of a cognition of non-difference is established—just like the cognition of mother-of-pearl as silver.
For in those cases where the cognition of non-difference occurs precisely while one is determining their difference, [the error is evident].
In that case, the recourse to a universal (sāmānya) is justified by the impossibility of explaining [the phenomenon] otherwise.
Furthermore, even for one who maintains that sounds are impermanent, it is not accepted that there is a direct determination of difference with respect to phonemes at every utterance.

Now, one might object: "In cases such as mother-of-pearl and silver, the linguistic usage of non-difference is appropriate because of the non-apprehension of difference; thus, a universal is impossible."
Because a sublating cognition arises in the case of "this is not silver," whereas here, since the existence of a universal is possible, the postulation of an error is entirely without basis,
as there is no sublating cognition such as "this is not the letter *ga*."
It is said:
the postulation of error does not depend solely upon a subverting cognition,
but also depends upon defects in the cause.
And it has been observed that error arises from the non-apprehension of difference due to extreme similarity; therefore,
even when a sublation does not arise immediately,
the determination of an illusion is entirely logical.
Therefore, movement and the like are not possible in that case.
Because it is observed immediately after effort, it is designated as "produced by effort" (*prayatnajam*).
Furthermore, the hearing of a sound immediately following human effort can be conceived in two ways: either because it was previously unperceived due to not having arisen, or...
It is either produced by effort and thus becomes perceptible, or it is manifested because it was previously unmanifested.
In this regard, first of all, it is not possible for effort to be the manifester of sound.
961 Something is manifested either by the removal of an obscuration or by its proximity;
however, an obscuration of sound is not logically possible.
For an obscuration such as a wall is observed to obstruct the connection between a sense organ and an object like a jar;
however, it is impossible to obstruct the connection between a sense organ and sound, because sound is eternal.
Indeed, obstruction consists in the prevention of origination or cessation.
And this [nature] is not possible for that which is eternal.
For the auditory faculty is indeed space, because it possesses sound;
and its possession of sound is due to its being the perceiver of sound, just like the visual faculty.
Just as the eye is the perceiver of form because it possesses form, so too is the ear possessed of sound;
and since space possesses sound, that very [space] is the ear.
Furthermore, since the word-sound possesses those qualities and is eternally inherent in it,
there is no possibility of its being veiled; therefore, its manifestation does not occur through the removal of such a veil.
For this very reason, proximity is impossible, because that which is to be manifested is eternally present.
Furthermore, manifestors located in the same place manifest simultaneously those objects that are not perceptible by multiple sense organs.
Just as lamps and other such objects [reveal] form and so forth,
form, dimension, and number— all of these are manifested simultaneously by lamps and the like.
Therefore, the perception of all sounds would indeed be unavoidable.
Furthermore, since sound is a specific quality of space (*ākāśa*),
and because space is one, a sound manifested by someone staying in Srughna would be perceived even by someone staying in Pāṭalīputra.
Furthermore, there would never be a cessation of perception.
If it is maintained that the manifestation of sound occurs only when the auditory faculty is in contact [with it], that too is not tenable.

What, indeed, is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense-faculty? It cannot be the removal of an obstruction, as in the case of opening [the eyes], because—as before—there is no possibility of an obstruction [in the first place].
Nor can it be a nourishment, as light provides for the ocular ray or for the internal winds.
Furthermore, because conjunction with parts is impossible for space,
the auditory organ, once refined, would manifest all sounds;
for an eye opened toward a jar does not fail to perceive a cloth.
"Ślokavārttika, Śabdanityatādhikaraṇa, verses 60–61. Therefore, since its being manifested is untenable, if it were not also caused by effort, [it would follow that it is eternal].
In that case, its perception dependent upon that [effort] would not be possible.
Therefore, the following inference should be formulated: Sound is produced by human effort, because, while not being manifested by it, it is perceived immediately after it;
for whatever is not manifested by something is perceived immediately after it.
That [sound] is produced by that [effort],
just as a jar is produced by the operation of the potter's wheel. But in what manner is sound produced by effort?

Regarding this, some say: sound, which inheres in itself, is produced by the air-particles set in motion by human effort; these particles strike specific locations, are refined by the resulting *saṃskāra* (potency), and are assisted by non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) known as conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) that extend in all directions.
Furthermore, because air possesses motion...

The sound initiated by that [object] also possesses motion; it is perceived when it comes into contact with the space delimited by the cavity of the ear, which has attained the state of the sense of hearing (*śrotra*).

Since the motion of air is dependent upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called "impetus" (*vega*), when that [impetus] ceases, the motion is interrupted; thus, for one whose sense of hearing is at a distance—
In that case, because it is not in close proximity, the sound would not be heard;
yet this is not tenable— for if sound were composed of air,
it would be perceived by those who are deaf through the sense of touch.
It might be thought: "Because it is overwhelmed, it is not perceived by touch.
That is not so;
for if it were indeed overwhelmed, [it would follow that it could never be perceived].
In that case, it would not be perceived by the auditory organ either.
Nor should it be said that air is not graspable by the tactile organ, because air is understood through its conformity with [the sound].
Now, if it is thought that only touch is perceived by the tactile faculty,
and not the substance of air—
that is not so; for even when distinct from touch, the substance is recognized.
Others, however, say: the first sound is produced either from conjunction or from disjunction.

Just as sound is generated in space from the conjunction of air and space, assisted by the conjunction of air with the palate and other [articulatory organs], so too, sound initiates another sound in space itself from the disjunction of air and space, aided by the disjunction of air from the palate and other [organs].

That too is another sound; thus, when the space delimited by the cavity of the ear has attained the state of the auditory organ (*śrotra*), the sound that has been produced is heard. (Verse 3) Because effort is observed to be manifold, and because there is a diversity of sounds, sound is a product (*kārya*) due to its own distinctness.
Furthermore—if sound were manifested by effort, it would not be perceived as distinct with every individual effort.
Indeed, even when there is a difference in the manifesting lamps, objects are not perceived as being manifold;
rather, it is well established that a difference in the producing cause is the cause of a difference in the effect.
Therefore, it is determined that effort produces the sound.

Just as the establishment of a difference in the effect is unimpeded when it follows upon a difference in the characteristics of the causal factors (*kāraka*), so too, even in the case of manifestation, a difference in the manifested cannot possibly exist through a difference in the manifestor.
As for sound, since it is perceived as being soft or strong when the effort [producing it] is soft or strong, it does not forfeit its status as an effect of that effort;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Since the cognition of that [sound] in the word is clear, the establishment of its perception will be justified by the postulation of various manifestors. (4)

If we are able to clearly demonstrate the recognition of the word-sound, then, once the effort's status as a producer has been refuted and its status as a manifestor established, [the sound will be proven eternal].
We shall explain the establishment of perception through the multiplicity of manifestors.
It is the auditory organ itself that is refined,
and its state of being refined is precisely its state of manifesting that [sound].
For the internal air rises up due to its conjunction with the self accompanied by effort.

Rising from the navel, it is refined by striking against the eight locations beginning with the chest; proceeding as far as its momentum allows, upon reaching the ear, it initiates a refinement conducive to the perception of sound.
The refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) is precisely that conjunction;
and because the air possesses velocity,
when the action [of the air] arises, the conjunction ceases due to the disjunction from the auditory organ.
There is an interruption in the perception of sound immediately following [the initial articulation].

Furthermore, due to the diversity of effort, the resulting diversity in the movement of the air, and the lack of uniformity in the conjunctions with the points of articulation such as the chest and so forth, there is a corresponding variation in the hearing of the sound.
Even the proponent of the production of sound (śabdotpattivādin) certainly accepts this diversity in the producers.

Otherwise, a difference in effects would be impossible. As for what was stated— that the eye, prepared by the act of opening, does not cause the perception of unperceived objects located in the same place according to their respective distinctions—
that is incorrect, because in that case the manifesting agent is one.

For indeed, a single opening [of the eyes] initiates the refinement of the eye that is conducive to the perception of everything; how then could perception be restricted? In this case, however, the unity of the refinements is unestablished.
Now, if that which is manifested is perceptible by a single sense organ, it follows that the manifestor must also be of the same nature;
for those things which are perceptible by the same sense organ [must share that characteristic].
Among those [sounds], there is only one manifestor from the very beginning,
just as light is for jars and other objects. And if the manifestor were one, the established order of perception would not be possible.

Therefore, since manifestation is impossible and its status as a causal agent is established, it is logically correct to conclude that recognition is based solely on the non-apprehension of difference.
To this it is replied: there would be apprehension by a single sense-faculty, and there would also be a distinction among the manifestors.
What is illogical here?
For that which possesses an essential relation and pervasion is a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For the determination of a natural connection and pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through the exclusion of all suspected limiting conditions (*upādhi*);
however, in this case, it cannot be ascertained whether, because jars and the like are perceived by a single sense organ,
there is a single manifestor for both them and the color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities residing within them.
Furthermore, because it possesses material substance (*rūpidravyatva*) and because it is inherent in that [substance],

the property of being perceivable by a single sense organ (*ekendriyagrāhyatva*), whose relationship and pervasion (*sambandhavyāpti*) are thus not established, is incapable of proving the identity of the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*).
Therefore, even though effort is a manifestor, the establishment of its perception is logically possible.
But surely, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists merely in the removal of the stagnant air; and once that has been removed, [the sound is perceived].
The perception of all sounds would be unavoidable.
It is said in reply: the removal of an obstruction is not its manifestor, because it is impossible for sound to be obstructed by air.
What is the use of depending on something unseen?

Furthermore, the established order of perception is fully accounted for by the distinction between the wood that removes [the obstruction] and the air, as well as by the distinction in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the division of the stable air.
Moreover, we do not describe the removal of the stable air as the latent impression.
However, it is indeed the conjunction with the abdominal air [that is the cause],
because that occurs first.
Why, then, did the author of the Bhāṣya state, "the other airs are motionless"?
It is for the purpose of destroying the momentum of the abdominal air.
Since it is understood elsewhere that the destruction of momentum results from contact with a tangible substance,
the mention of "stable air" (*sthiravāyu*) in the Bhāṣya here is also solely for that purpose.
But surely, since space is one and it is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), when that [space] is refined, because all the sense organs of all persons would be refined, everyone would perceive sound.
This is not a fault;
for the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is the refinement of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), and since the ear-cavities differ for each individual person, [there is no contradiction].
One whose ear-cavity is not conditioned does not perceive sound;
furthermore, one perceives sound from a great distance when it is carried by a following wind,
because the force of the internal air, aided by the impulsion of the external wind, becomes the cause for its travel over a long distance.
But in the view that one sound initiates another sound, the following wind serves no purpose at all.
Due to the diversity of the manifestors, the sound appears as if it were manifold, just as the moon appears so to those with ophthalmia due to the different movements of their eyes. (5)
If that [single] apprehension were clear, then the perception of diversity in sound would indeed be unestablished;

however, by means of various manifesting agents— namely, the internal winds arising from various speakers— which, being mutually independent, initiate distinct refinements of the auditory organ and thereby produce the cognition of diverse sounds,
the sound is perceived as if it were manifold.
Like the moon [perceived through various apertures], when there is perception in various locations by means of visual functions pierced by darkness, everyone’s consensus is one of error;
for it is only sound that has entered the cavity of the ear which is actually heard.
As for what is said— that because sound is an effect, it is perceived in various locations due to the difference in the locations of its causes— that is incorrect;
even though sound is produced, [it is not as you claim].

Nevertheless, because it would follow that sounds from both proximate and distant sources would be perceived simultaneously, and because there would be no distinction between [perception] with the wind blowing toward one and with the wind blowing away from one, the sense organ does not perceive what has reached it.
Even if there were contact, the sense organ does not travel to the location of the sound;

for the ear is perceptible as being located within the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), and otherwise, it would follow that perception would be identical whether the wind blows toward or away from the listener.

But when a sound is perceived upon reaching the path of the ear, a difference in location is cognized; therefore, this is an illusion—the notion that the sound is perceived in various locations. What is the basis for this illusion?
We say that it is dependent on the location of the manifestor.
For it is the internal air, in dependence upon its impact with the locations such as the palate and so forth, that manifests [the sound].
Therefore, the location of the speaker also becomes the location of the manifestor.
Therefore, for one hearing a sound, the location of its manifestor also becomes present in the intellect, being postulated as invariably concomitant with it.
Furthermore, its distance or proximity is determined by the specific nature of the sound's manifestation.
And in cases where the speaker is perceived through direct observation, the specific direction is necessarily ascertained from the particularity of the auditory perception of the sound.
Therefore, there is also the conceptualization of specific directions;
however, for one who is not capable of such discrimination,
a delusion regarding the location of the manifestor is indeed observed.
And thus, because the sense organs are incapable of perceiving themselves, when a sound is apprehended by the auditory organ, its location is not grasped; rather,
the place of its utterance is what is perceived, and it is understood as being situated there.

This delusion is indeed consistent with the fact that it initiates linguistic usage based on the comprehension of sounds as they occur in various locations. Furthermore, a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phonemes is not admitted; for such a [perceived] state arises through the delusion caused by the smallness or greatness of the sounds (*nāda*). (Verse 7)
Since it has been established that effort does not produce phonemes when their perception is already manifest,

and since it has been determined that sounds are merely manifested— given the rule that they are perceived immediately after [the effort]— a sound neither increases nor decreases, because the increase or decrease of a manifestor cannot be the cause of an increase or decrease in the manifested object.
However, when there is a powerful effort, a great wind is produced;
its many constituent parts come into contact with numerous peripheral portions of the circular ear-cavity.
Consequently, due to the multiplicity of these manifesting conjunctions, [the sound is perceived as loud].

Because there is a multiplicity of simultaneous perceivers, and because the intervals between them are not perceived, the sound appears as if it were large, just as a forest appears large because the spaces between the trees are not perceived.
When those particles of air are joined together either suddenly or gradually, then the perception [of sound] is also rapid or slow.
Or it is protracted;
for when there is a closure of the palate and other articulatory points during their pronunciation, then,
in accordance with that, the perception of the phoneme also occurs as lasting for only one mātrā.
The establishment of the conventional usage of "short" vowels occurs when the state of being more opened or less closed pertains specifically to the palate and other articulatory points.
In that case, since the cognition of the phoneme itself increases in duration, the conventional usage of "long" phonemes is established;

for in the linguistic usage of elders, it is observed that the expression of meaning occurs in accordance with that [duration], and the status of being a signifier is likewise accepted on that very basis.

Nor is there the fault of impermanence in this designation, because it is the phoneme (*varṇa*) as qualified by its specific adjuncts (*upādhi*) that constitutes the expressive signifier (*vācaka*), and thus that [qualified entity] is impermanent. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in the impermanence of the sequence of phonemes, since the phonemes themselves, which serve as the expressive signifiers when possessing a particular sequence, are eternal.
Now, if the manifestation of sound is momentary,

how is its apprehension possible? For it is only when an object such as a jar is perceived that, by virtue of it, the latent impression (saṃskāra) deposited by previous experience is awakened, and the recognition "this is that very same one" arises.
But when a sound has been uttered and has vanished, how can recognition arise at a later time?
To this he says: "The awakening of its latent impression does not necessarily depend solely upon the perception of that [sound]."
Therefore, from a latent impression (saṃskāra) awakened by another cause, there arises the apprehension of that [object]. // 8 //
For if this were the rule— that the perception of that [object] alone is the cause for the awakening of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—
then recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of sound would not be possible; however,
latent impressions have causes for their awakening that are not restricted [to the perception of the object itself].
Recognition of the sound will occur at the very moment of the first encounter due to a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by the force of other causes.
Is it not the case that the cognition “this is that same letter *ga*” is the apprehension of that [identity], and not merely the non-apprehension of difference?
How is this determined?
For it is observed that, due to the non-apprehension of difference, there arises the cognition "this very thing is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.
To this, he replies: "When there is no means of knowledge for the difference, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver, etc. (Verse 996).
In that case, by what means can the apprehension of it, which is established through common experience, be denied? // 9 //

For when a means of valid cognition clearly establishes the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver, it is postulated that the perception of non-difference arises because the distinction is not apprehended due to their similarity;
however, in the case of sound, the difference with each utterance is not established by direct perception.
How is it not established?
Is it not the case that a phoneme (varṇa) is perceived as distinct through its large or small magnitude? It is not so.
Even though one perceives largeness and smallness,
it is only the largeness and smallness that appear as distinct within the cognition of the phoneme, not the phonemes themselves;
nor can their difference be apprehended even by inference, as has already been explained.

Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition for difference, this [cognition] is non-different despite appearing as if divided; this is established solely by the force of direct perception itself. // 9 //
But surely, by the very force of that [prior] apprehension, inference is refuted; and if inference is refuted, then that apprehension [itself] is refuted—
thus there is a circular dependency.
Regarding this, he says: "By the refutation of inference, its status as a means of apprehension is established;
since it is established by one's own direct experience, the suspicion of error is averted. (10)
The suspicion that this error is based on the non-apprehension of difference is removed by the refutation of inference alone; however,
since the apprehension of that [identity] is established by the force of direct experience (*pratīti*), it does not depend on any other cause—
so how could there be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*)?

Now, one might ask: why is it that the inference of difference in the flame is not refuted by the force of that [perceptual] apprehension? To this he says: "Without a difference in the flames, the expansion of appearances would not be possible; however, recognition is justified by similarity due to the non-apprehension of difference. (11)
The flame is a composite whole (*avayavin*).
Every composite whole is produced through the conjunction of its own parts and perishes through their destruction.
For a cloth produced by the interlacing of threads is seen to perish when those threads are separated;
and light existing within the interior of a house and such places is a fiery form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, qualities such as color and so forth, which depend upon a substance, do not exist apart from that substance.

Therefore, one must accept that luminous atoms (*taijasa-paramāṇu*), although not perceived because they are constantly overwhelmed, remain present right up to the extent of the light's diffusion as established by direct perception.
And when these [atoms] have reached another location, this must be admitted: their conjunctions fall apart.
When those [atoms] have been disjoined and the substance initiated by them has also perished,
the perception of a flame is not possible without the perception of another flame.
Recognition based on the non-apprehension of difference is established as an error, since it is observed in cases such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
however, nothing is impossible without a difference in words.
Therefore, according to the method of reasoning already stated, the apprehension of that [identity] is accepted here.
It has already been explained how the fact of being perceived immediately after an effort is possible even without a difference [in the word] upon each pronunciation; thus,
recognition is free from opposition.
Therefore, because it is neither existent nor non-existent as a cause, sound is eternal;
for this very same nature of eternality is also accepted in the case of space and other such entities. (13)
Effort alone is conceived as the cause of sound;
and since that effort is established as being merely a manifestor through the force of recognition upon seeing [the same] *dvija* and so forth,
it must be a manifestor even at the first perception.
Therefore, since sound exists while being devoid of a cause, it is eternal like the sky and so forth;
thus, it is not impermanent.
This *Nyāyaśuddhi*, which establishes the eternity of sound according to the view of the teacher Prabhākara, has been proclaimed by Śālikanātha as verse 1005.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Purification of Logic" (*Nyāyaśuddhi*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra. 1006.
